title: Prompt Engineering
meta: This is a trigger file, not study material. Question visible → answer OUT LOUD → then expand → grade what you missed.

questions.text: What is a prompt actually doing to the model?
points: A prompt = the conditioning prefix of an autoregressive model
System, instructions, examples, context → all just tokens it attends to
You steer a distribution, you don't instruct an agent
That's why it's engineerable: versionable, cacheable, testable
Mapping prefix → behaviour is learned, not specified → measure, don't assume
questions.flow: prefix → attention → next-token distribution → steer, then measure
questions.trap: "I tell the model what to do"

questions.text: Walk me through the anatomy of a production prompt.
points: Six parts, in order: role · task · context · constraints · examples · output contract
Order is not style: stable content first (cacheable), volatile last
Each part answers one question: who, what, with what, what's forbidden, what shape
Most under-built part: the output contract — it also lives in your parser
Past ~3k tokens shared by features → split it

links.label: Anatomy of a production prompt
links.target: 08-Prompt-engineering/02-Core Prompt Anatomy & Techniques/10-Anatomy of a production prompt

questions.flow: role → task → context → constraints → examples → output contract
questions.trap: one paragraph of instructions with the format tacked on

questions.text: System prompt, user turn, assistant prefill — what goes where?
points: Roles are one token stream with markers; weight comes from training
System: identity, task, constraints you'd hate to see overridden
User: untrusted input, delimited as data
Prefill: seed the assistant turn to force a format or skip preamble
Role markers are a contract, not a security boundary

links.label: System prompt vs user prompt vs assistant prefill
links.target: 08-Prompt-engineering/02-Core Prompt Anatomy & Techniques/18-System prompt vs user prompt vs assistant prefill

questions.flow: system = policy → user = data → prefill = shape
questions.trap: treating the system prompt as access control

questions.text: Zero-shot, few-shot, or many examples — how do you decide?
points: Start zero-shot with a precise instruction; add examples only on evidence
0 → 1 is the big jump: one example pins the output shape
Plateau around 4–8 examples on most tasks
Costs grow linearly: tokens, order sensitivity, label bias
Example count = a hyperparameter tuned against an eval
questions.flow: zero-shot → one for shape → few for edge cases → stop at plateau
questions.trap: more examples is always better

questions.text: Prompts as code, or prompts as config?
points: As code: in the repo, PR-reviewed, ships with the parser that reads its output
As config: in a registry, changes without a deploy, non-engineers can edit
Deciding axis: does prompt change velocity exceed deploy cadence? Who holds the pen?
Output-contract changes stay coupled to code either way
Config needs its own review, eval gate and rollback

links.label: Prompts as code vs prompts as config
links.target: 08-Prompt-engineering/09-Prompt Ops/83-Prompts as code vs prompts as config

questions.flow: who edits + how often → code or registry → contract stays with code
questions.trap: "registry, so anyone can hot-fix prod" with no gate

questions.text: Why do people say evaluation is the whole of prompt engineering?
points: Results move on spurious features: formatting, example order
Reading 20 outputs can't separate a real gain from sampling noise
Everything downstream needs a metric: optimisation, CI gates, model upgrades
The eval set outlives the prompt — the durable asset
No eval → every edit is an untested change

links.label: Why prompt eval is the whole discipline
links.target: 08-Prompt-engineering/08-Evaluation & Testing Prompts/73-Why prompt eval is the whole discipline

questions.flow: collect real inputs → define correct → metric → then edit prompts
questions.trap: "I iterated until the outputs looked good"

questions.text: Why does chain-of-thought work — and when does it hurt?
points: Compute: fixed work per token → a derivation buys more forward passes
State: written steps re-enter context → step 4 reads step 2
Gains are narrow: maths and symbolic reasoning, not classification or extraction
Cost: reasoning tokens are output tokens — priced high, generated serially
The chain is not an execution trace; it can be unfaithful
questions.flow: more tokens = more compute + external state → helps multi-step → costs latency
questions.trap: "it makes the model think harder" / reading the chain as the explanation

questions.text: How do you choose few-shot examples? Static block or retrieved per query?
points: Four axes: similarity, diversity, difficulty, label balance
Order matters too — same examples permuted can swing accuracy
kNN retrieval per query beats a fixed block: demonstrations fit the input
Same index and retriever as RAG; payload is demonstrations, not documents
Catch: a changing block kills prefix caching

links.label: Dynamic retrieved few shot (kNN example selection)
links.target: 08-Prompt-engineering/02-Core Prompt Anatomy & Techniques/14-Dynamic retrieved few-shot (kNN example selection)

questions.flow: labelled store → retrieve similar → balance labels → order → measure
questions.trap: hand-picking three easy examples and never revisiting

questions.text: Why are prompts brittle? What does prompt sensitivity look like?
points: Performance is a distribution, not a point
Same meaning, different separator or example order → different accuracy
Cause: the model conditions on token sequences, not meanings
Few-shot adds priors from recency and label frequency
Discipline: evaluate over variants, then pin the exact rendered prompt
questions.flow: paraphrase the prompt → measure spread → pick robust variant → pin it
questions.trap: quoting one prompt's score as "the" accuracy

questions.text: How does provider prompt caching work, and how do you order a prompt for it?
points: Caches the KV state of a prefix → skips its prefill
It's a prefix cache: first differing token invalidates everything after
Order: tool schemas → system → examples → retrieved chunks → history → turn
Reads are a fraction of input price; writes cost more; entries expire in minutes
Per-request text in the system prompt = cache miss every call

links.label: Context ordering for prompt cache hit rate
links.target: 08-Prompt-engineering/05-Context Engineering/48-Context ordering for prompt-cache hit rate

questions.flow: stable first → volatile last → mark breakpoints → watch hit rate
questions.trap: interpolating the timestamp or user name at the top

questions.text: What is DSPy actually optimising?
points: Idea: program the pipeline, compile the prompts
Signature (inputs → outputs) + module (CoT, ReAct) + optimiser
Optimiser writes instructions and picks few-shot demos against your trainset and metric
MIPROv2: bootstraps demos from passing traces, proposes instructions, searches combinations
Needs a metric you trust — otherwise it optimises noise
questions.flow: signature → module → metric + trainset → compile → re-compile on model change
questions.trap: "DSPy writes better prompts" with no metric

questions.text: Self-consistency — what's the mechanism and what does it cost?
points: Sample N chains at temperature > 0, extract answers, majority vote
Wrong reasoning disagrees with itself; correct reasoning converges
Cost: a strict N× token multiplier
Only works when answers are comparable enough to vote on
Bonus: vote share = a confidence signal
questions.flow: sample N → extract answers → vote → use agreement as confidence
questions.trap: using it for free-text answers that can't be voted

questions.text: Tool descriptions are prompts." What makes a good one?
points: It's read at the moment of the call decision
Say: what it does, when NOT to use it, each parameter, what it doesn't return
Several sentences, not a one-line label
Schema is prompt too: parameter names and enums constrain harder than prose
Overlapping tools → wrong-tool calls; fix descriptions before the model

links.label: Tool descriptions as prompts
links.target: 08-Prompt-engineering/06-System Prompts & Agent Instructions/58-Tool descriptions as prompts

questions.flow: purpose → when not → parameters → returns → test tool-selection accuracy
questions.trap: one-line descriptions, then blaming the model for wrong calls

questions.text: What does role or persona prompting actually change?
points: It shifts register, tone and vocabulary reliably
It does not add knowledge the model lacks
Accuracy effect of "you are an expert" is small and inconsistent → measure
Useful part of a role: audience and task framing, not flattery
Persona text is not a guardrail
questions.flow: role sets register → task + constraints do the work → test with and without
questions.trap: "you are a world-class expert" as a quality lever

questions.text: Temperature 0 with a seed — is that deterministic prompting?
points: Temp 0 = argmax: removes sampling randomness only
Batching + non-associative floating point → logits can differ run to run
A near-tie flips one token → the rest of the output diverges
Batch-invariant serving exists, at a throughput cost
Design for it: compare fields with tolerance, cache approved outputs
questions.flow: temp 0 → still batch-dependent → near-tie flips → test on structure, not strings
questions.trap: promising byte-identical output

questions.text: Prompt, RAG, fine-tune or tool — which lever for which gap?
points: Four levers fix four different gaps — diagnose first
Prompt: behaviour within a request; free to iterate
RAG: facts that change, need attribution
Fine-tune: stable, high-volume behaviour, format, tone
Tool: anything it shouldn't guess — live data, maths, writes

links.label: Prompting vs Fine tuning vs RAG vs Tool use
links.target: 08-Prompt-engineering/01-Foundations & Mental Model/03-Prompting vs Fine-tuning vs RAG vs Tool-use

questions.flow: name the gap → behaviour / knowledge / action → cheapest lever first
questions.trap: fine-tuning to add knowledge

questions.text: JSON mode, schema-constrained decoding, or parse-and-repair?
points: JSON mode: parses; says nothing about your keys or types
Schema-constrained: grammar masks illegal tokens → shape by construction
Guarantee covers shape, not meaning; void on refusal or truncation
Repair loop: feed the validation error back — new information, not a resample
Never repair silently: count repairs as a metric
questions.flow: constrain shape → validate meaning → bounded repair → fallback → measure
questions.trap: "structured output means it's correct"

questions.text: One big prompt, or a chain of small ones?
points: Chain when one prompt holds too many jobs (extract → judge → draft)
Each stage gets focused context, its own eval, retry policy, cheaper model
Costs: latency adds, errors compound, an orchestration layer to run
Chain = a fixed DAG you designed; agent = model picks the next step
Split where you can write a test for the intermediate output
questions.flow: one job per call → test each stage → watch compounding error + latency
questions.trap: chaining by default, or calling a chain an agent

questions.text: Reasoning model with a short prompt, or a standard model with prompted CoT?
points: Reasoning models run their own thinking phase; budget is a dial
Prompted scaffolds ("think step by step", decomposition) become redundant or harmful
Give them the goal, constraints and success criteria, not the steps
Pay in latency and thinking tokens → route only hard requests
Standard model + CoT still wins on cheap, well-understood tasks
questions.flow: task difficulty → route → reasoning model: goal only · standard: scaffold
questions.trap: porting a CoT prompt unchanged to a reasoning model

questions.text: Hand-tune prompts or auto-optimise them?
points: Hand-tuning breaks: combinatorial space, noisy eyeballing, non-local edits
An optimisation run is an inference workload: candidates × trials × trainset
Benefit: a few metric points, decays on model change
Rule: optimise high-traffic, stable prompts; hand-tune low-traffic or changing ones
The eval harness pays off even if you never optimise
questions.flow: build the eval → hand-tune → optimise only stable high-volume prompts
questions.trap: auto-optimising before an eval exists

questions.text: Long context: instruction at the top or the bottom?
points: Short prompts: placement is noise
Long: attention favours start and end → bulk data first, instruction last
Cheap hedge: state it at both ends
Tension: caching wants the stable instruction first
Resolve: stable policy up top (cached), the specific question at the bottom
questions.flow: stable policy first → documents → question + key instruction last
questions.trap: burying the question above 20k tokens of documents

questions.text: Assertions or an LLM judge for testing prompts?
points: Assertions first: schema valid, citation present, figures in source, length
Free, exact, unbiased, no calibration
Assert on the contract, not the prose — exact-match on free text = flaky
Judge only where the property needs judgement; pairwise > pointwise
A judge is a prompt too → validate against human labels

links.label: LLM as judge for prompt quality

questions.flow: code checks → judge for the rest → calibrate judge → gate
questions.trap: judging everything with an uncalibrated LLM

questions.text: Big model with a simple prompt, or a small model with a heavily engineered one?
points: Prototype on the strong model to prove the task is possible
Small models need more structure: explicit format, examples, shorter steps
Route by difficulty: cheap model for easy requests, frontier where it changes the answer
Costly failure = under-routing: hard query, confident wrong answer
Each prompt is tuned to one model — it isn't portable
questions.flow: prove on big → distil the prompt down → route → eval per model
questions.trap: one prompt assumed to work across model sizes

questions.text: Offline regression suite or online A/B test for a prompt change?
points: Both, in order: offline gates the release, online checks user value
Offline CI is stochastic and non-local → thresholds must absorb run-to-run variance
Tier it: assertions per commit → judge checks → full suite on release candidates
A/B: split by user or session, never by request
Measure behaviour: completion, escalation, thumbs-down — with clustered errors

links.label: Regression suites & CI for prompts
links.target: 08-Prompt-engineering/08-Evaluation & Testing Prompts/78-Regression suites & CI for prompts

links.label: A B testing prompts in production
links.target: 08-Prompt-engineering/08-Evaluation & Testing Prompts/79-A-B testing prompts in production

questions.flow: assertions → judge → full suite → canary → A/B on behaviour
questions.trap: shipping on an A/B split per request with naive statistics

questions.text: Should prompt releases be decoupled from code releases?
points: Service resolves a label (production), never a version
Ship = move the label; rollback = move it back
MTTR for a bad prompt: deploy time → cache TTL
Cost: version skew — two versions live for one TTL
Fine for tone; fatal for output-contract changes → those ship with code

links.label: Decoupling prompt release from code release
links.target: 08-Prompt-engineering/09-Prompt Ops/86-Decoupling prompt release from code release

questions.flow: label → resolve at runtime → move label to release → contract changes with code
questions.trap: hot-swapping a prompt that changes the output schema

questions.text: More instructions, or more examples?
points: Instructions state the rule; examples show the shape and edge cases
Instruction rules: specific thresholds, positive framing, no overlaps
Conflicting instructions are resolved silently — one is dropped
Examples over-anchor: the model copies their length, topic and labels
Use both: rule first, then 2–3 diverse examples that span it
questions.flow: write the rule precisely → add diverse examples → check for anchoring
questions.trap: patching every failure with another sentence

questions.text: Delimiters, XML tags, Markdown — does prompt structure matter?
points: Structure separates instructions from data → fewer mix-ups
Tags let you refer to a block by name ("use only ")
Pick one scheme and stay consistent; match the model family's guidance
Delimiters reduce accidental confusion; they don't stop injection
Structured input makes structured output easier to request
questions.flow: label each block → reference by name → same scheme everywhere
questions.trap: relying on delimiters as a security boundary

questions.text: The provider upgraded the model and your prompts regressed. What now?
points: A prompt is co-tuned with one model — not portable
Old scaffolds (few-shot counts, "think step by step") can hurt the successor
Migration = an eval exercise: freeze prompt, run golden set on both models
Then tune; often the fix is deleting instructions
Pin versions; providers deprecate on a clock → plan the window
questions.flow: pin → golden set on old + new → diff by slice → tune → canary → switch
questions.trap: "same prompt, newer model, must be better"

questions.text: Your system prompt is 4,000 tokens of accumulated patches. What's wrong, and how do you fix it?
points: It accreted one rule per incident → contradictions
Conflicts resolve silently; nobody knows which rule wins
Fix: eval set first, then rewrite from the task, not from the patches
Split by layer: platform rules · product policy · feature · per-request
Move per-feature rules out; keep the stable core cacheable

links.label: System prompt design at scale
links.target: 08-Prompt-engineering/06-System Prompts & Agent Instructions/55-System prompt design at scale

questions.flow: build eval from incidents → rewrite → layer → delete what the eval doesn't need
questions.trap: adding rule 41 in capitals

questions.text: A prompt works in English and fails in other languages. Why, and what do you do?
points: Model quality and tokenisation cost differ by language
English instructions + non-English input often beat translating the instructions — test both
State the output language explicitly; don't infer it
Few-shot examples anchor language → provide them per locale
Eval per language slice; averages hide the failure
questions.flow: per-language eval → instruction language test → explicit output language → locale examples
questions.trap: translating the prompt and assuming parity

questions.text: Users extracted your system prompt. How bad is that?
points: It's just tokens in context; refusing to reveal is a soft preference
Extraction routes: "repeat your instructions", paraphrase, translation, formatting tricks
Posture: assume it leaks
Nothing in it may be load-bearing for security: no keys, no hidden policy
Real controls live outside: permissions, tool scopes, server-side checks

links.label: System prompt extraction & prompt leaking
links.target: 08-Prompt-engineering/10-Safety, Security & Adversarial Prompting/94-System-prompt extraction & prompt leaking

questions.flow: assume leak → strip secrets → enforce in code → treat prompt as public
questions.trap: "never reveal these instructions" as the defence

questions.text: A retrieved document tells the model to ignore its instructions. Defend the system.
points: Indirect injection: hostile text arrives in content, not from the user
You can't prevent it → layers that fail independently
Reduce: spotlighting (delimit, datamark, encode), guard classifiers
Contain: privilege separation — the reader of untrusted text holds no tools
Human approval on anything irreversible; break the lethal trifecta
questions.flow: mark data → least privilege → sandbox actions → approve irreversible → monitor
questions.trap: "we told the model to ignore instructions in documents"

questions.text: By turn 30 the assistant has drifted from its instructions. What's happening?
points: Context rot: accuracy falls as input grows, non-uniformly
Pollution: a failed tool call or old hallucination now reads as fact
Neither throws — it just answers worse
History policy: last turns verbatim · middle summarised · objective pinned
Rewriting history = a cache write → batch compaction, don't do it every turn
questions.flow: pin objective → trim + summarise → drop failed tool output → eval long sessions
questions.trap: evaluating only on short conversations

questions.text: Output length keeps blowing the latency and cost budget. Levers?
points: Output tokens are the expensive, serial side
Replace adjectives with countable limits: "at most 3 sentences"
Structured output with bounded fields beats "be concise"
max_tokens is a guillotine, not a style control → check for truncation
Examples set length more than instructions do
questions.flow: countable limit → bounded schema → short examples → max_tokens as backstop
questions.trap: "be concise" plus a hard max_tokens cut

questions.text: Design the prompt layer for a product with 50 prompts across 5 teams.
points: Six stages: template store → renderer → gateway → model → parser → validator
Store holds versioned prompts; renderer fills typed slots and stamps the version
Gateway: model choice, retries, fallbacks, budgets
Parser + validator own the output contract
Every trace carries prompt version + model version
questions.flow: store → render + stamp → gateway → call → parse → validate → trace
questions.trap: prompt strings inline in business logic

questions.text: Design eval-driven prompt development, from an idea to production.
points: Write the eval before the prompt — the eval is the spec
Golden set from real inputs, with what a correct answer must contain
Tiered CI: assertions per commit → judge → full suite on release candidates
Release by label; canary, then A/B on behaviour
Production failures flow back into the golden set

links.label: Regression suites & CI for prompts
links.target: 08-Prompt-engineering/08-Evaluation & Testing Prompts/78-Regression suites & CI for prompts

questions.flow: real inputs → eval → prompt → CI gate → canary → A/B → failures back to eval
questions.trap: prompt first, eval "later"

questions.text: Four hundred tenants each want their own tone and rules. Design the prompts.
points: One versioned template with typed slots, not 400 prompts
Slots: tone, forbidden topics, glossary, schema name, locale
Per-tenant config rows you can validate and diff
Roll out by tenant tier via labels
Tenant text is untrusted input → sanitise slot values
questions.flow: one template → typed slots → tenant config → validate → staged rollout
questions.trap: forking the prompt per tenant

questions.text: Cost-model a prompt at a million calls a day. What are the levers?
points: Four terms: input, output, cache reads, cache writes — different prices
Output is the expensive side → verbosity control beats context trimming
Large stable prefix becomes cheap once cached
Three caches: provider prefix · exact-result · semantic (can answer the wrong question)
Route by difficulty; batch what isn't interactive
questions.flow: tokens × price per term → cut output → cache prefix → route → batch
questions.trap: trimming the system prompt while outputs run long

questions.text: Who can change a production prompt, and what's the audit trail?
points: Prompt change = behaviour change → same rigour as code
Roles: author, reviewer, approver; domain experts can propose
Gate: eval pass before the label moves
Audit: who, what diff, which eval run, when the label moved
Every response traceable to prompt + model version
questions.flow: propose → review → eval gate → label move → trace per response
questions.trap: anyone with registry access editing production

questions.text: Tell me about a prompt that failed in production and how you debugged it.
points: Open with the decision the prompt served and the symptom
Show the rendered prompt that actually ran — not the template
Classify: instruction conflict · missing context · format · model change
The fix and the eval case you added so it can't return
<fill: the system, the symptom, the number before → after>
questions.flow: symptom → rendered prompt → classify failure → fix → eval case → number
questions.trap: "I rewrote it until it worked"
